source.title: On the Invariance and Generality of Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Xing Han; Liu Ziyin; Suchi Saria; Paul Pu Liang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling under information-preserving and information-losing data transformations. It reports largely invariant scaling for bijective transformations, but weaker curves and saturation under non-bijective transformations, refining the scope of a single standard scaling law.
record.gate_note: The text also gives theoretical propositions and cites prior scaling-law results; those are not recorded as empirical rows. Table 2 predictions and comparisons are included where they report fitted scaling parameters. Values visible only in figures are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-form laws on its own sweeps: Llama-style LMs (~0.8M–657M params, 100K–3B tokens), ViT, ResNet, Wav2Vec2 and MIMIC-IV classifiers. Bijective re-encodings leave the fitted curves nearly unchanged. Information-losing transformations (quantization, low-rank projection, noise, corpus shift) change the fitted β and raise the loss floor E. This bears on V1, V5 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling laws are invariant under bijective transformations and modified predictably under non-bijective ones via information resolution ρ. They say a law fit on a source domain can be transported to a target domain. The 'within 3%' figure refers to the data exponent β only. The predicted floor E is less accurate, e.g. a 0.41 gap in the cross-corpus setting, though closer than the baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines theoretical information-resolution modeling with scaling sweeps over transformed data and several modalities. It does not reproduce the original sources' model-and-token/compute sweeps as such.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling behavior changes with transformation type and information resolution: bijective transformations leave curves largely invariant, while quantization, low-rank projection, and noise or corpus shifts alter curves or loss floors. In cross-corpus prediction, the estimated information resolution and its estimator also affect predicted loss floors.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed dataset size, the loss-minimising model capacity shrinks as information resolution ρ falls. Shown for WikiText-103, OpenWebText and MIMIC-IV (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal model size for a given dataset decreases with data information content.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), as stated in the text
record.problems: Several transformation-curve results are qualitative and visible only in figures, without numerical exponents or uncertainty estimates. Experiments generally use 4–6 capacities and 5–6 dataset sizes; the paper itself notes limitations in transferring transformation parameters and estimating information resolution across domains.
record.rows_left_out: No additional empirical results bearing on the listed versions were omitted. Theoretical propositions, transformation formulas, and cited findings from prior work were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Compute axis and runs beyond ~657M params. Tests are on small models, and the power-law form is assumed and fitted, not compared to alternatives.
No small-to-large extrapolation; the predictions are cross-domain, not cross-scale.
No compute-optimal frontier. Figure 3 varies capacity at fixed dataset size only.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.

missing.what: ImageNet-1K cross-domain tables: under quantization the real β is 0.197 and E 4.46, against source βs 0.28 and Es 2.29. Under noise injection the real β is 0.252 and E 2.732, against βs 0.31 and Es 2.34.
MIMIC noise ρ=0.25: ground-truth β 0.193 and E 4.146, against clean ≈0.323/1.49.
Choice of ρ estimator (vocab, 3-gram, compress) changes the predicted E gap from 0.856 to 0.412 against real E 4.413.
missing.versions: V7 (method sensitivity of the study's own predictor; context only)

record.verdict_notes: Many of the record's rows encode comparisons of the authors' predictor with baselines. For the claim, only the 'Real' fitted values matter, compared with source-domain fits from the appendix tables. Table 2 'Real' E values disagree with the appendix ground truth (2.6533 vs 2.36; 3.7833 vs 3.378). All model scales are small: LMs ≤657M, many below 10M. The bijective-invariance results would also limit V7 (not every data change moves exponents), but those rows are kept on V1/V5 to avoid conflicting states. Quantization lowers NLL by shrinking the vocabulary, which confounds raw loss comparisons in R4–R6.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments test scaling mainly across model capacity and dataset size, not a broad compute sweep; the claimed several-orders-of-magnitude range is not established for every setting.
The cross-domain forecasts are not tests of small-run fits predicting runs orders of magnitude larger.
The paper gives a theoretical compute-optimal formula and varies capacity at fixed dataset size, but does not empirically test how optimal parameter and token counts vary with compute.
No controlled comparison isolates depth, width, or architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Tests include vision and speech, as well as clinical time series and cross-corpus or corruption settings. Video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer to downstream tasks are not tested.
The study does not test whether pretraining loss predicts downstream-task performance.

The study tests sensitivity to data transformations and information resolution, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, or fitting method, nor compare published exponents across those choices.

rows.subject: MIMIC-IV in-hospital mortality prediction scaling sweep
rows.size_stated: 10 model capacities in the capacity experiment
rows.operation_detail: Measure fitted data-scaling exponent β and irreducible loss for clean and noise-degraded clinical time-series data.
rows.measure: Empirical fitted data-scaling exponent β
rows.value: Real: 0.2843; Quality-Aware: 0.2975; Sub-Optimal: 0.2933; Ours: 0.2961
rows.note: The table compares the empirical fit with predictions from the proposed framework and two baselines.
rows.check: Only the 'Real' value (β=0.2843) is a result bearing on the claim; the clean source βs is about 0.322 (Table 6). Quality-Aware, Sub-Optimal and Ours are the study's method versus baselines and should not set the state. The subject is a MIMIC-IV time-series classifier, not an LM, so drop V1.

rows.value: Quality-Aware: 1.8314; Sub-Optimal: 1.8285; Ours: 2.7842

relationships.condition: Small Llama-style LMs on WikiText-103, OpenWebText, C4, untransformed and under bijective re-encodings
relationships.reason: Fitted scaling curves are reported as nearly identical to baseline, exponents within fitting noise; figure-only (R1–R3).
relationships.display_finding: Fitted scaling curves remain nearly identical to baseline under bijective re-encodings, with exponent differences within fitting noise.

relationships.condition: ViT/ImageNet, ResNet/CIFAR-100, Wav2Vec2/LibriSpeech, clean and bijectively transformed inputs
relationships.reason: Scaling exponents are reported preserved within fitting noise; qualitative, figure-only (R7, R9, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Scaling exponents were reported to remain unchanged within fitting noise across the vision and speech experiments.

relationships.condition: Information-losing transformations: quantization, low-rank projection, noise injection, corpus shift
relationships.reason: Fitted β and loss floor E shift with the data, e.g. MIMIC β 0.32→0.24 and E 1.49→3.78; OWT→MIMIC E 2.80→5.14 (R4–R6, R8, R10, R12–R20).
relationships.display_finding: On MIMIC, transformations shifted β from 0.32 to 0.24 and E from 1.49 to 3.78; moving from OWT to MIMIC shifted E from 2.80 to 5.14.
